name: Expansive steam specification
summary: Watt's 1782 patent explained cutting off steam early in each stroke and letting it expand, saving fuel; Sadi Carnot discussed his example in his 1824 study of heat engines.
description: Watt specifies cutting off admission during the stroke and using steam expansion for the remainder, with a quarter-stroke example and an approximate pressure/work calculation.
tier_reason: A bounded technical contribution, transmission episode or documented configuration useful within a specific history; no broad dependence claim is established.

impact.note: One patent text setting out a fuel-saving refinement known to the engine trade, with a few successors including Carnot's use of its example.

why: Fuel was a major running cost for engine users, and Boulton and Watt's income depended on the fuel their engines saved.

date.basis: Patent granted 12 March; specification enrolled 4 July 1782.

events.statement: Watt specifies cutting off admission during the stroke and using steam expansion for the remainder, with a quarter-stroke example and an approximate pressure/work calculation.
events.caveats: This node dates the specification, not first conception or first use. Its inverse-volume steam-pressure approximation is historical, not adopted as a generally correct steam model.

evidence.locator: Section 26: introductory dates; First New Improvement; figure 1 and quarter-stroke calculation
evidence.supports: Admission cutoff, expansive action, numerical example and 1782 specification date.

events.statement: Carnot reproduced and critically discussed Watt’s quarter-stroke table from the 1782 patent.
events.scope: Watt’s 1782 steam-admission cutoff and quarter-stroke pressure/work table.
events.caveats: Practical expansive working before 1824 does not by itself establish use of this exact calculation; Carnot’s discussion is critical, not unqualified acceptance.

evidence.locator: Note 27, printed pp. 100–101 and surrounding discussion
evidence.supports: Names the 1782 patent, reproduces its quarter-stroke table and critiques the approximation.

evidence.locator: 1782 specification, expansion section and quarter-stroke example
evidence.supports: Identifies the configuration and numerical example.

links.statement: Watt's expansive-engine specification explicitly reuses his condenser system and hot-cylinder arrangement while adding admission cutoff and expansion.
links.scope: Watt's 1782 specification, definitions and First Improvement.
links.alternatives: Expansion was also possible in other engine configurations; this edge concerns Watt's specified arrangement.
links.caveats: Continuation of a design system, not a claim that separate condensation is universally required for expansion.
links.timing: The 1769 specified components are explicitly incorporated into the later 1782 specification.

evidence.locator: Section 26: definitions Third/Fourth; First Improvement, figures 1–2
evidence.supports: Identifies condensers as Watt's invention and keeps the cylinder hot while specifying expansion.

links.statement: The principle of cutting off steam admission and using expansion applied at Shadwell was also specified by Watt in 1782.
links.scope: The Shadwell engine and Watt’s own 1782 specification.
links.alternatives: Other mechanisms, makers or applications could serve similar purposes.
links.caveats: This comparison establishes continuity of a named principle, not that the particular Shadwell engine was the sole cause of the specification.
links.timing: Dates attach to the scoped event or source described, not automatic global primacy.
